prompt:
Let $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. Suppose that $f$ has infinitely many zeros, but there is no $x\in(a,b)$ with $f(x)=f'(x)=0$.

(a) Prove that $f(a)f(b)=0$.

(b) Give an example of such a function on $[0,1]$.
answer: (a) An accumulation point $c$ of the zeros is a zero with $f'(c)=0$ if $c\in(a,b)$, so $c\in\{a,b\}$. (b) $f(x)=x\sin\frac1x$ for $0<x\le1$, $f(0)=0$.

solutions.title: Accumulation point of the zeros
solutions.body:
**(a)** Choose a sequence of pairwise distinct zeros of $f$. By Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a subsequence $z_m\to c\in[a,b]$, and discarding at most one term we may assume $z_m\ne c$ for all $m$. By continuity $f(c)=\lim f(z_m)=0$.

If $c$ were in $(a,b)$, $f$ would be differentiable at $c$ and
$$f'(c)=\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{f(z_m)-f(c)}{z_m-c}=\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{0-0}{z_m-c}=0,$$
so $f(c)=f'(c)=0$ with $c\in(a,b)$, which is excluded. Hence $c=a$ or $c=b$, so $f(a)=0$ or $f(b)=0$, i.e. $f(a)f(b)=0$.

**(b)** Let
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}x\sin\dfrac1x,&0<x\le1,\\[2mm]0,&x=0.\end{cases}$$
It is continuous on $[0,1]$ (at $0$ because $|f(x)|\le x$) and differentiable on $(0,1)$ with $f'(x)=\sin\frac1x-\frac1x\cos\frac1x$. It vanishes at the infinitely many points $x=\frac1{k\pi}$, $k=1,2,\dots$. If $f(x)=0$ for some $x\in(0,1)$, then $\sin\frac1x=0$, so $\cos\frac1x=\pm1$ and $f'(x)=\mp\frac1x\ne0$. So $f$ and $f'$ never vanish together in $(0,1)$. ∎

e0$ and $f(x)=f'(c)(x-c)+o(x-c)$, so $f(x)
e0$ for $0<|x-c|$ small: interior zeros are isolated.

The zero set $Z$ is closed, so $Z\cap I$ is compact; each of its points has a neighbourhood containing no other zero, and finitely many of these neighbourhoods cover $Z\cap I$. So $f$ has only finitely many zeros, a contradiction. Hence $f(a)f(b)=0$.

prompt: Let $k$ and $n$ be positive integers. A sequence $(A_1,\dots,A_k)$ of $n\times n$ real matrices is *preferred* by Ivan the Confessor if $A_i^2\ne0$ for $1\le i\le k$, but $A_iA_j=0$ for $1\le i,j\le k$ with $i\ne j$. Show that $k\le n$ in all preferred sequences, and give an example of a preferred sequence with $k=n$ for each $n$.
answer: Pick a column $v_i$ of $A_i$ with $A_iv_i\ne0$; since $A_iv_j=0$ for $i\ne j$, the $v_i$ are linearly independent, so $k\le n$. Example: $A_i=E_{ii}$ (single $1$ at position $(i,i)$).

solutions.title: Independent columns
solutions.body:
For each $i$, $A_i^2\ne0$, so some column of $A_i^2=A_i\cdot A_i$ is non-zero; that column is $A_iv_i$ where $v_i\in\mathbb R^n$ is the corresponding column of $A_i$. So $A_iv_i\ne0$. For $j\ne i$, $A_iv_j$ is a column of $A_iA_j=0$, so $A_iv_j=0$.

Suppose $c_1v_1+\dots+c_kv_k=0$. Applying $A_i$:
$$0=\sum_{j=1}^kc_j\,A_iv_j=c_i\,A_iv_i,$$
and since $A_iv_i\ne0$, $c_i=0$. So $v_1,\dots,v_k$ are linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb R^n$, and $k\le n$.

**Example with $k=n$:** let $A_i=E_{ii}$ be the matrix with a single $1$ in position $(i,i)$ and zeros elsewhere. Then $A_i^2=A_i\ne0$ and $A_iA_j=0$ for $i\ne j$. ∎

which forces $k\le n$. The example $A_i=E_{ii}$ shows $k=n$ is attained. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Also let $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ and $b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n$ be real numbers such that $a_i+b_i>0$ for $i=1,2,\dots,n$. Prove that
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{a_ib_i-b_i^2}{a_i+b_i}\le\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^na_i\cdot\sum_{i=1}^nb_i-\Big(\sum_{i=1}^nb_i\Big)^2}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i+b_i)}.$$
answer: Using $\frac{XY-Y^2}{X+Y}=Y-\frac{2Y^2}{X+Y}$ on both sides, the inequality becomes $\sum\frac{b_i^2}{a_i+b_i}\ge\frac{(\sum b_i)^2}{\sum(a_i+b_i)}$, the Engel form of Cauchy–Schwarz.

solutions.title: Rewrite and apply Cauchy–Schwarz
solutions.body:
For $X+Y\ne0$ we have the identity
$$\frac{XY-Y^2}{X+Y}=\frac{Y\big((X+Y)-2Y\big)}{X+Y}=Y-\frac{2Y^2}{X+Y}.$$
Apply it with $X=a_i$, $Y=b_i$ to each term on the left, and with $X=\sum a_i$, $Y=\sum b_i$ to the right side (note $\sum(a_i+b_i)>0$):
$$\text{LHS}=\sum_{i=1}^nb_i-2\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{b_i^2}{a_i+b_i},\qquad \text{RHS}=\sum_{i=1}^nb_i-2\,\frac{\left(\sum_ib_i\right)^2}{\sum_i(a_i+b_i)}.$$
So the inequality is equivalent to
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{b_i^2}{a_i+b_i}\ge\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^nb_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i+b_i)},$$
which is the Engel form of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $\sum\frac{x_i^2}{y_i}\ge\frac{(\sum x_i)^2}{\sum y_i}$ ($y_i>0$) with $x_i=b_i$, $y_i=a_i+b_i$. (Proof: by Cauchy–Schwarz, $\left(\sum x_i\right)^2=\left(\sum\frac{x_i}{\sqrt{y_i}}\sqrt{y_i}\right)^2\le\sum\frac{x_i^2}{y_i}\sum y_i$.) ∎

solutions.title: Sum-of-squares identity
solutions.body:
After the reduction of the first solution it suffices to show, for $s_i=a_i+b_i>0$ and $S=\sum s_i$,
$$S\sum_i\frac{b_i^2}{s_i}-\Big(\sum_ib_i\Big)^2\ge0 .$$
Expanding both products as double sums over $(i,j)$,
$$S\sum_i\frac{b_i^2}{s_i}-\Big(\sum_ib_i\Big)^2=\sum_{i,j}\left(\frac{s_j}{s_i}b_i^2-b_ib_j\right).$$
The diagonal terms $i=j$ vanish; grouping the terms $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$ for $i<j$,
$$\frac{s_j}{s_i}b_i^2+\frac{s_i}{s_j}b_j^2-2b_ib_j=\frac{(s_jb_i-s_ib_j)^2}{s_is_j}\ge0 .$$
So the expression equals $\sum_{i<j}\frac{(s_jb_i-s_ib_j)^2}{s_is_j}\ge0$, proving the inequality (with equality iff all ratios $b_i/(a_i+b_i)$ are equal). ∎

prompt:
Let $n\ge k$ be positive integers, and let $\mathcal F$ be a family of finite sets with the following properties:

(i) $\mathcal F$ contains at least $\binom nk+1$ distinct sets containing exactly $k$ elements;

(ii) for any two sets $A,B\in\mathcal F$, their union $A\cup B$ also belongs to $\mathcal F$.

Prove that $\mathcal F$ contains at least three sets with at least $n$ elements.
answer:
Take $ inom nk+1$ $k$-sets ("generators") with union $V$, $|V|>n$. An element in at most $ inom{n-1}{k-1}$ generators ("appropriate") is avoided by $\ge inom{n-1}k+1$ generators, whose union has $\ge n$ elements; double counting shows any $n$ elements contain an appropriate one. Pick appropriate $v_1\in V$, get $U_1
ot
i v_1$; pick appropriate $v_2\in U_1$, get $U_2
ot
i v_2$. Then $V,U_1,U_2$ are distinct.

solutions.title: Generators and appropriate elements
solutions.body:
**Case $n=k$.** There are two distinct $n$-element sets $A,B\in\mathcal F$; then $A\cup B\in\mathcal F$ has more than $n$ elements, so $A,B,A\cup B$ are three such sets. Assume now $n>k$.

Fix $N=\binom nk+1$ distinct $k$-element sets of $\mathcal F$, the *generators*. By (ii), the union of any non-empty collection of generators lies in $\mathcal F$. Let $V$ be the union of all generators. A set with $m$ elements has $\binom mk$ subsets of size $k$; we use repeatedly:

> if a union of generators contains more than $\binom{m}{k}$ of them, then it has more than $m$ elements.

Since $V$ contains $N>\binom nk$ generators, $|V|\ge n+1$.

Call $v\in V$ *appropriate* if $v$ lies in at most $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ generators. Then at least $N-\binom{n-1}{k-1}=\binom{n-1}{k}+1\ (\ge1)$ generators avoid $v$; their union $U(v)\in\mathcal F$ contains more than $\binom{n-1}k$ generators, so $|U(v)|\ge n$, and $v\notin U(v)$.

**Claim.** Among any $n$ elements $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of $V$ there is an appropriate one. Otherwise each $x_i$ lies in at least $\binom{n-1}{k-1}+1$ generators. Count pairs $(G,x_i)$ with $G$ a generator and $x_i\in G$: there are at least $n\binom{n-1}{k-1}+n=k\binom nk+n$ of them, but each generator contains at most $k$ of the $x_i$, giving at most $kN=k\binom nk+k$ pairs. Since $n>k$, this is a contradiction.

**Three large sets.** As $|V|\ge n+1$, $V$ has an appropriate element $v_1$; let $U_1=U(v_1)$, so $|U_1|\ge n$ and $v_1\notin U_1$. As $|U_1|\ge n$, $U_1$ contains an appropriate element $v_2$; let $U_2=U(v_2)$, so $|U_2|\ge n$ and $v_2\notin U_2$. Now
* $V\ne U_1$ since $v_1\in V\setminus U_1$;
* $U_2\ne V$ and $U_2\ne U_1$ since $v_2\in U_1\subseteq V$ but $v_2\notin U_2$.

So $V,U_1,U_2$ are three distinct members of $\mathcal F$ with at least $n$ elements. ∎

prompt:
Let $S_n$ denote the set of permutations of the sequence $(1,2,\dots,n)$. For every permutation $\pi=(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_n)\in S_n$, let $\operatorname{inv}(\pi)$ be the number of pairs $1\le i<j\le n$ with $\pi_i>\pi_j$; i.e. the number of inversions in $\pi$. Denote by $f(n)$ the number of permutations $\pi\in S_n$ for which $\operatorname{inv}(\pi)$ is divisible by $n+1$.

Prove that there exist infinitely many primes $p$ such that $f(p-1)>\frac{(p-1)!}{p}$, and infinitely many primes $p$ such that $f(p-1)<\frac{(p-1)!}{p}$.
answer: With $G(x)=\sum_\pi x^{\operatorname{inv}\pi}=\prod_{j=1}^{p-1}\frac{1-x^j}{1-x}$ and $\varepsilon=e^{2\pi i/p}$: $f(p-1)-\frac{(p-1)!}p=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}(1-\varepsilon^k)^{1-p}$, whose sign is dominated by $k=1,p-1$; it is $>0$ for $p\equiv3$ and $<0$ for $p\equiv1\pmod 4$. Both classes contain infinitely many primes.

solutions.title: Roots of unity filter
solutions.body:
**Generating function.** Let $G_n(x)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}x^{\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}$. Then
$$G_n(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{n}(1+x+\dots+x^{j-1}).$$
(Induction on $n$: inserting $n$ into a permutation of $1,\dots,n-1$ in one of the $n$ possible positions adds $n-1,n-2,\dots,0$ inversions.)

**Filter.** Let $p$ be an odd prime, $n=p-1$, $\varepsilon=e^{2\pi i/p}$. Since $\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\varepsilon^{km}$ is $p$ if $p\mid m$ and $0$ otherwise,
$$f(p-1)=\frac1p\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}G_{p-1}(\varepsilon^k)=\frac{(p-1)!}{p}+\frac1p\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}G_{p-1}(\varepsilon^k).$$

**Evaluate $G_{p-1}(\varepsilon^k)$, $1\le k\le p-1$.** As $\varepsilon^k\ne1$,
$$G_{p-1}(\varepsilon^k)=\prod_{j=1}^{p-1}\frac{1-\varepsilon^{jk}}{1-\varepsilon^k}=\frac{\prod_{m=1}^{p-1}(1-\varepsilon^m)}{(1-\varepsilon^k)^{p-1}}=\frac{p}{(1-\varepsilon^k)^{p-1}},$$
because $jk$ runs over all non-zero residues mod $p$, and $\prod_{m=1}^{p-1}(z-\varepsilon^m)=1+z+\dots+z^{p-1}$ equals $p$ at $z=1$. Hence
$$D:=f(p-1)-\frac{(p-1)!}{p}=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}(1-\varepsilon^k)^{-n}\qquad(n=p-1\text{ even}).$$

**Real form.** With $\theta_k=\pi k/p\in(0,\pi)$: $1-\varepsilon^k=1-e^{2i\theta_k}=2\sin\theta_k\,e^{i(\theta_k-\pi/2)}$. Since $n$ is even, $e^{in\pi/2}=(-1)^{n/2}$, so
$$(1-\varepsilon^k)^{-n}=(-1)^{n/2}\,\frac{e^{-in\theta_k}}{(2\sin\theta_k)^n}.$$
The terms for $k$ and $p-k$ are complex conjugates, so
$$D=\frac{(-1)^{n/2}}{2^n}\,T,\qquad T=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{\cos(n\theta_k)}{\sin^n\theta_k}.$$

**Sign of $T$.** $\cos(n\theta_k)=\cos(\pi k-\theta_k)=(-1)^k\cos\theta_k$. For $k=1$ and $k=p-1$ this equals $-\cos\frac\pi p$, so these two terms contribute $-\dfrac{2\cos(\pi/p)}{\sin^n(\pi/p)}<0$. For $p=3$ there are no other terms. For $p\ge5$, the other $p-3$ terms have $\sin\theta_k\ge\sin\frac{2\pi}p=2\sin\frac\pi p\cos\frac\pi p$, so their total absolute value is at most $\dfrac{p-3}{\sin^n(\pi/p)\,(2\cos(\pi/p))^n}$. This is smaller than the main term because
$$(2\cos\tfrac\pi p)^{p}\ge\Big(2\cos\frac\pi5\Big)^p=\varphi^p>p-3\qquad(\varphi=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}2)$$
(true for $p=5$: $\varphi^5>11$, and $\varphi^{p+1}-\varphi^p=\varphi^{p-1}\ge1$). Hence $T<0$ for every odd prime $p$, and
$$\operatorname{sign}D=-(-1)^{(p-1)/2}=\begin{cases}+1,&p\equiv3\pmod4,\\-1,&p\equiv1\pmod 4.\end{cases}$$

(Check: $p=3$: $f(2)=1>\frac23$; $p=5$: $f(4)=1+3=4<\frac{24}5$.)

By Dirichlet's theorem (or the elementary proofs for these two progressions) there are infinitely many primes $p\equiv3\pmod4$, for which $f(p-1)>\frac{(p-1)!}p$, and infinitely many primes $p\equiv1\pmod4$, for which $f(p-1)<\frac{(p-1)!}p$. ∎

prompt:
Let $(x_1,x_2,\dots)$ be a sequence of positive real numbers satisfying $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{x_n}{2n-1}=1$. Prove that
$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty\sum_{n=1}^k\frac{x_n}{k^2}\le2.$$
answer: Swap the sums: the left side is $\sum_nx_n\sum_{k\ge n}\frac1{k^2}$, and $\sum_{k\ge n}\frac1{k^2}<\sum_{k\ge n}\frac1{k^2-1/4}=\frac1{n-1/2}=\frac2{2n-1}$.

solutions.title: Interchange and telescope
solutions.body:
All terms are positive, so we may interchange the order of summation:
$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty\sum_{n=1}^k\frac{x_n}{k^2}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n\sum_{k=n}^\infty\frac1{k^2}.$$
For each $k\ge1$,
$$\frac1{k^2}<\frac1{k^2-\frac14}=\frac1{k-\frac12}-\frac1{k+\frac12},$$
so, by telescoping,
$$\sum_{k=n}^\infty\frac1{k^2}<\frac1{n-\frac12}=\frac2{2n-1}.$$
(Equivalently: $1/x^2$ is convex, so $\frac1{k^2}<\int_{k-1/2}^{k+1/2}\frac{dx}{x^2}$, and summing gives $\int_{n-1/2}^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2}$.) Therefore
$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty\sum_{n=1}^k\frac{x_n}{k^2}<\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n\cdot\frac{2}{2n-1}=2\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{x_n}{2n-1}=2 .$$ ∎

prompt: Today, Ivan the Confessor prefers continuous functions $f\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(x)+f(y)\ge|x-y|$ for all pairs $x,y\in[0,1]$. Find the minimum of $\int_0^1f$ over all preferred functions.

solutions.title: Pair $x$ with $x+\frac12$
solutions.body:
**Lower bound.** For $0\le x\le\frac12$ put $y=x+\frac12$: $f(x)+f(x+\frac12)\ge\frac12$. Integrating over $[0,\frac12]$,
$$\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=\int_0^{1/2}\Big(f(x)+f\big(x+\tfrac12\big)\Big)dx\ge\int_0^{1/2}\frac12\,dx=\frac14 .$$

**The bound is attained.** Let $f(x)=\left|x-\frac12\right|$, which is continuous. By the triangle inequality
$$|x-y|\le\Big|x-\tfrac12\Big|+\Big|\tfrac12-y\Big|=f(x)+f(y),$$
so $f$ is preferred, and
$$\int_0^1\Big|x-\tfrac12\Big|dx=\frac18+\frac18=\frac14 .$$

**Answer: $\frac14$.** ∎

solutions.title: Pair $x$ with $1-x$
solutions.body:
Taking $y=1-x$ gives $f(x)+f(1-x)\ge|1-2x|$ for all $x\in[0,1]$. Integrate over $[0,1]$; since $\int_0^1f(1-x)\,dx=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx$,
$$2\int_0^1f\ge\int_0^1|1-2x|\,dx=\frac12,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\int_0^1f\ge\frac14 .$$
The function $f(x)=|x-\frac12|$ satisfies $f(x)+f(y)\ge|x-y|$ by the triangle inequality and has integral exactly $\frac14$, so the minimum is $\frac14$.

**Answer: $\frac14$.** ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer, and denote by $\mathbb Z_n$ the ring of integers modulo $n$. Suppose that there exists a function $f\colon\mathbb Z_n\to\mathbb Z_n$ satisfying the following three properties:

(i) $f(x)\ne x$,

(ii) $f(f(x))=x$,

(iii) $f(f(f(x+1)+1)+1)=x$ for all $x\in\mathbb Z_n$.

Prove that $n\equiv2\pmod 4$.
answer: $f$ is a fixed-point-free involution, so $n$ is even and $\operatorname{sgn}f=(-1)^{n/2}$. With $g(x)=f(x+1)$, (iii) says $g^3=\mathrm{id}$, so $g$ is even; the shift $x\mapsto x+1$ is an $n$-cycle, hence odd; so $f$ is odd and $n/2$ is odd.

solutions.title: Signs of permutations
solutions.body:
By (ii), $f\circ f=\mathrm{id}$, so $f$ is a bijection of $\mathbb Z_n$ and an involution; by (i) it has no fixed point. Hence $\mathbb Z_n$ splits into the 2-element orbits $\{x,f(x)\}$, so $n$ is even and $f$ is a product of $n/2$ disjoint transpositions:
$$\operatorname{sgn}(f)=(-1)^{n/2}.$$

Let $s(x)=x+1$ and $g=f\circ s$, i.e. $g(x)=f(x+1)$. Then $g(g(g(x)))=f(f(f(x+1)+1)+1)$, so (iii) says $g^3=\mathrm{id}$. Thus $\operatorname{sgn}(g)^3=1$, and since $\operatorname{sgn}(g)=\pm1$, $g$ is even.

The permutation $s$ is a single cycle of length $n$, so $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=(-1)^{n-1}=-1$ (as $n$ is even). Since $f=g\circ s^{-1}$,
$$\operatorname{sgn}(f)=\operatorname{sgn}(g)\operatorname{sgn}(s)^{-1}=-1 .$$
So $(-1)^{n/2}=-1$, i.e. $n/2$ is odd, which means $n\equiv2\pmod4$.

*Remark.* Such $f$ exist for every $n\equiv2\pmod 4$; for $n=2$ take $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=0$. ∎

prompt: Let $k$ be a positive integer. For each nonnegative integer $n$, let $f(n)$ be the number of solutions $(x_1,\dots,x_k)\in\mathbb Z^k$ of the inequality $|x_1|+\dots+|x_k|\le n$. Prove that for every $n\ge1$, we have $f(n-1)f(n+1)\le f(n)^2$.
answer: Call a positive sequence *good* if $a(m-1)/a(m)$ is non-decreasing. The sequence $\binom{n+k}{k}$ is good, and $a\mapsto a(m)+a(m-1)$ preserves goodness; since $\sum f(n)q^n=\frac{(1+q)^k}{(1-q)^{k+1}}$, $f$ is good. (Alternatively, induct on $k$ via $f_k(n)=\sum_{m\le n}\big(f_{k-1}(m)+f_{k-1}(m-1)\big)$.)

solutions.title: Generating function and a ratio-preserving step
solutions.body:
For a sequence of positive numbers $a(0),a(1),\dots$ set $a(-1)=0$ and call it **good** if the ratios $r(m)=\frac{a(m-1)}{a(m)}$ are non-decreasing for $m\ge1$, i.e. $a(m-1)a(m+1)\le a(m)^2$ for $m\ge1$. We must show that $f$ is good.

**Generating function.** Summing $q^{|x_1|+\dots+|x_k|+c}$ over $x\in\mathbb Z^k$ and $c\ge0$ (each $(x,c)$ with $|x|_1+c=n$ corresponds to one solution counted in $f(n)$):
$$\sum_{n\ge0}f(n)q^n=\Big(\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z}q^{|x|}\Big)^k\frac1{1-q}=\Big(\frac{1+q}{1-q}\Big)^k\frac1{1-q}=\frac{(1+q)^k}{(1-q)^{k+1}}.$$

**Step 0.** $\frac1{(1-q)^{k+1}}=\sum_n g_0(n)q^n$ with $g_0(n)=\binom{n+k}{k}$, and $\frac{g_0(n-1)}{g_0(n)}=\frac{n}{n+k}$ is increasing, so $g_0$ is good.

**Multiplying by $1+q$ preserves goodness.** If $a$ is good, let $b(m)=a(m)+a(m-1)$ (the coefficients of $(1+q)\sum a(m)q^m$). For $m\ge1$, dividing numerator and denominator by $a(m-1)$,
$$\frac{b(m-1)}{b(m)}=\frac{a(m-1)+a(m-2)}{a(m)+a(m-1)}=\frac{1+r(m-1)}{1+1/r(m)}$$
(for $m=1$ read $r(0)=0$). As $m$ increases, $r(m-1)$ does not decrease and $1/r(m)$ does not increase, so this ratio is non-decreasing: $b$ is good.

Applying this $k$ times to $g_0$ gives the coefficients of $\frac{(1+q)^k}{(1-q)^{k+1}}$, namely $f$. So $f$ is good:
$$f(n-1)f(n+1)\le f(n)^2\quad(n\ge1).$$ ∎

solutions.title: Induction on the dimension
solutions.body:
Use the notion "good" from the first solution. Let $f_k$ denote the function for dimension $k$, and $f_0\equiv1$ (only the empty tuple), which is good.

**Recursion.** Fixing $x_k=c$ with $|c|\le n$ leaves $f_{k-1}(n-|c|)$ solutions, so
$$f_k(n)=f_{k-1}(n)+2\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}f_{k-1}(m)=\sum_{m=0}^{n}h(m),\qquad h(m)=f_{k-1}(m)+f_{k-1}(m-1)$$
(with $f_{k-1}(-1)=0$). If $f_{k-1}$ is good, then $h$ is good by the "multiply by $1+q$" step of the first solution. It remains to show:

**Partial sums of a good sequence are good.** Let $a$ be good and $S(m)=\sum_{j=0}^ma(j)$. We need $S(m-1)S(m+1)\le S(m)^2$. Writing $S(m+1)=S(m)+a(m+1)$ and $S(m-1)=S(m)-a(m)$, this is equivalent to
$$a(m+1)\,S(m-1)\le a(m)\,S(m).$$
For $0\le j\le m-1$, goodness gives $\frac{a(j)}{a(j+1)}\le\frac{a(m)}{a(m+1)}$, i.e. $a(j)a(m+1)\le a(j+1)a(m)$. Summing over $j$,
$$a(m+1)S(m-1)\le a(m)\big(S(m)-a(0)\big)\le a(m)S(m).$$

Hence $f_k$ is good whenever $f_{k-1}$ is, and by induction $f_k(n-1)f_k(n+1)\le f_k(n)^2$ for all $k\ge1$, $n\ge1$. (For $k=1$ this is $(2n-1)(2n+3)\le(2n+1)^2$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ be a $n\times n$ complex matrix whose eigenvalues have absolute value at most 1. Prove that
$$\|A^n\|\le\frac{n}{\ln 2}\|A\|^{n-1}.$$
(Here $\|B\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\|Bx\|$ for every $n\times n$ matrix $B$ and $\|x\|=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^2}$ for every complex vector $x\in\mathbb C^n$.)
answer: Cayley–Hamilton with $|c_k|\le\binom nk$ gives $\|A^n\|\le(1+r)^n-r^n$ ($r=\|A\|$); combine with $\|A^n\|\le r^n$ and split at $r_0=\frac1{2^{1/n}-1}<\frac n{\ln2}$. (Even $\|A^n\|\le n\|A\|^{n-1}$ holds, by Schur triangularisation and induction.)

solutions.title: Cayley–Hamilton and two bounds
solutions.body:
Let $r=\|A\|$. If $r=0$ then $A=0$ and there is nothing to prove, so let $r>0$. Recall $\|XY\|\le\|X\|\|Y\|$, so $\|A^j\|\le r^j$.

**Bound 1.** Let $\chi(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n(t-\lambda_i)=t^n+c_1t^{n-1}+\dots+c_n$ be the characteristic polynomial. By Vieta, $c_k$ is $\pm$ the sum of the $\binom nk$ products of $k$ eigenvalues, each of modulus $\le1$, so $|c_k|\le\binom nk$. By Cayley–Hamilton, $A^n=-(c_1A^{n-1}+\dots+c_nI)$, hence
$$\|A^n\|\le\sum_{k=1}^n\binom nk r^{n-k}=(1+r)^n-r^n .$$
**Bound 2.** $\|A^n\|\le r^n$.

Let $r_0=\dfrac1{2^{1/n}-1}$, the value where $(1+r)^n=2r^n$. Since $2^{1/n}-1=e^{\ln2/n}-1>\frac{\ln 2}n$, we have $r_0<\frac n{\ln2}$.

* If $r\le r_0$: $\|A^n\|\le r^n=r\cdot r^{n-1}\le r_0r^{n-1}<\frac n{\ln2}r^{n-1}$.
* If $r>r_0$: $\|A^n\|\le r^{n-1}\varphi(r)$ with $\varphi(r)=\dfrac{(1+r)^n-r^n}{r^{n-1}}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom nj r^{-(n-1-j)}$, a non-increasing function of $r>0$. Hence $\varphi(r)\le\varphi(r_0)=r_0\Big(\big(1+\tfrac1{r_0}\big)^n-1\Big)=r_0(2-1)=r_0$, because $1+\frac1{r_0}=2^{1/n}$. So again $\|A^n\|\le r_0r^{n-1}<\frac n{\ln 2}r^{n-1}$.

In both cases $\|A^n\|\le\frac n{\ln2}\|A\|^{n-1}$. ∎

solutions.title: Schur form and induction: $\|A^n\|\le n\|A\|^{n-1}$
solutions.body:
We prove the stronger bound $\|A^n\|\le n\|A\|^{n-1}$ (enough, since $\ln2<1$), by induction on $n$ (with $\|A\|^0=1$). For $n=1$, $A=(a)$ with $|a|\le1$.

Conjugating by a unitary matrix does not change norms, so by Schur's theorem we may assume $A$ is upper triangular; its diagonal entries $a_{11},\dots,a_{nn}$ are its eigenvalues, $|a_{ii}|\le1$. Write $A=X+Y+Z$, where $X=a_{11}E_{11}$, $Y$ is the rest of the first row ($a_{12},\dots,a_{1n}$ in row 1), and $Z$ is $A$ with its first row and column replaced by zeros, i.e. $Z=0\oplus A'$ with $A'$ the lower-right $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ block.

**Products.** Since $Y$ lives in row 1 and columns $2..n$, $X$ only at $(1,1)$, and $Z$ has zero first row and column:
$$Y^2=0,\quad YX=0,\quad ZX=0,\quad ZY=0 .$$
Hence $ZA=Z^2$ and $(Y+Z)A=YZ+Z^2=(Y+Z)Z$, and by repetition $(Y+Z)A^{n-1}=(Y+Z)Z^{n-1}$. So
$$A^n=XA^{n-1}+(Y+Z)A^{n-1}=XA^{n-1}+(Y+Z)Z^{n-1}.$$

**Norms.** $\|X\|=|a_{11}|\le1$. $Y+Z=AP$ with $P=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\dots,1)$ (the first column of $A$ is $a_{11}e_1$), so $\|Y+Z\|\le\|A\|$; and $Z=P(Y+Z)$, so $\|A'\|=\|Z\|\le\|A\|$. The matrix $A'$ is upper triangular with eigenvalues $a_{22},\dots,a_{nn}$, so by the induction hypothesis $\|Z^{n-1}\|=\|A'^{\,n-1}\|\le(n-1)\|A'\|^{n-2}\le(n-1)\|A\|^{n-2}$. Therefore
$$\|A^n\|\le\|A\|^{n-1}+\|A\|\cdot(n-1)\|A\|^{n-2}=n\|A\|^{n-1}\le\frac n{\ln2}\|A\|^{n-1}.$$ ∎
